reason: The court held that the notarial deed of gift could not be varied by oral evidence and that no notarial surrender of the appellant's rights existed.
The court made this factual finding on the evidence, but it is not a ratio-level legal rule.
The court read the two particular deeds together as part of the lex commissoria analysis, but the extracted statement is only a case-specific document finding.
The quote supports the disciplinary finding against the second respondent, but the statement drops the material distinction that the first respondent was cleared.
The court held that criminally charactered professional misconduct may justify disenrolment even without a criminal conviction.
The court decided the narrower pleading and prescription points, not a general rule that causes of action must be formulated in terms of relevant statutes.
The court treated this certificate under the Recovery of Loans by Banks Act as conclusive, not every certificate of sale issued under any statute.
The quote records how one preliminary issue should have been answered on the case facts, not a usable legal rule.
The court held that granting a tenancy declaration and ejectment without a prayer for that relief was in excess of jurisdiction.
The court held that the plaintiff's tenancy claim ended when he voluntarily surrendered possession to the new lessees.
The statement is too vague to capture the holding that monthly tenancy claims are outside a partition action under sections 5(a) and 48(1).
The court held that a monthly tenant's claim is outside the scope of a partition action and should be considered, if at all, at execution.
The court upheld this will because testamentary intention appeared from the instrument, not because any mix of testamentary forms is generally valid.
The court applied the principle that testamentary intention is gathered from the will's terms and surrounding circumstances.
The holding depended on a vesting order having been made before the applicant tenant died, which the statement omits.
The court stated specific categories of temple property and temple legal capacity, while the statement reduces that holding to an imprecise generality.
The ownership-evidence holding is supported, but the cited Land Settlement Ordinance section was not the provision construed for this rule.
The court upheld a specific Rule 14(1)(a) objection, not the broad proposition that any preliminary objection may be raised for breach of any rule.
The court held that Rule 14(1)(a) requires a plain and concise statement of facts and the alleged fundamental-right infringement.
The court held that slanderous and abusive pleading language negates compliance with public-law pleading guidelines.
The extracted statement is an incomplete fragment rather than a legal proposition decided by the court.
The statement is too vague to identify the Rent Act section 22(7) interpretation that controlled the appeal.
The quoted point formed part of the section 22(7) interpretation, but the statement omits the ownership-nexus limitation and statutory context.
The court held that the defendant failed to prove prescriptive title under section 3 of the Prescription Ordinance.
The statement is a tautological fragment and omits the Partition Law section 48 exceptions that made the actual holding useful.
